edge.title: The compensation that isn't cash
edge.setup: Part of your land, or your building's setback, is needed — for a road, a drain, a widening. Nobody offers you money. You are offered a certificate, a share of built-up area, extra floors, a credit you can sell on later. The officer is helpful, the paper looks official, and the number printed on it sounds larger than any cash you were expecting.
edge.tell: You hand over the asset today; the paper's price gets set by someone else, later.
move: Do not part with possession, a signature or an original deed until the certificate exists in your name. A sanction or an approval is not a certificate.
Ask in writing who buys this paper and at what discount to its face value — then ask a second buyer the same question.
Get face value and realisable value as two separate numbers, from someone who is not the party acquiring your asset.
Keep every acknowledgement with a date and an inward number. The delay, not the rate, is usually what costs you.
edge.why: Cash settles now, at a price you can verify. Paper settles later, at a price discovered in a thin market you are not part of. The mechanism is not fraud — it is a quiet transfer of timing risk and valuation risk from the body taking your asset onto you. Whoever controls when the paper converts controls what it is worth, and that is never the person holding it.
edge.variants: Same shape: a builder offering area-sharing instead of a sale price, a refund offered as store credit or a voucher, salary deferred into stock or a joining bonus, an 'assured bonus' on an insurance policy, dues settled as a future adjustment.

lens.name: Survivorship bias
lens.one_line: You only see the things that made it, so you learn the wrong lesson from them.
lens.detail: The classic case: WWII engineers wanted to armour the bullet holes on returning planes, until Abraham Wald pointed out those were the survivable hits — the armour belonged where returning planes had no holes, because planes hit there never came back. Every 'habits of successful people' list has the same flaw: the identically-behaving failures aren't available to interview.
elsewhere: Dropout-founder stories, drawn from the tiny surviving tail.
Fund performance tables that quietly exclude closed funds.
Old buildings seeming better built — the shoddy ones were demolished.
lens.test: Who is missing from this dataset because they didn't make it this far?
lens.today: The Hindu reports a speaker at the Bengaluru Skill Summit saying that the city's white-collar success has left a non-urban world behind. The Bengaluru you see in summits, launches and metro inaugurations is the part that worked; the people and places that did not keep up rarely appear in the sample. When someone says 'Bengaluru is doing great', ask who is missing from that picture.

moved.what: Karnataka has raised bus fares: BMTC by 35% and KSRTC and other corporations by 23%. The Times of India reports the BMTC minimum fare rising by up to ₹10 and the Bengaluru airport bus ticket at ₹425. Urban Acres says the BMTC hike starts 5 November.
moved.so_what: If you hold or buy a monthly BMTC pass, recompute your monthly cost before renewing. For a daily commuter, a 35% rise is a real monthly increase, so compare it against the metro for the same route.

moved.what: The Hindu reports that the partial opening of the Pink Line may increase congestion in Bengaluru. The metro's Pink Line is to be inaugurated by PM Modi on 13 November, according to several outlets.
moved.so_what: Do not assume the ceremony day means a smoother commute. Expect diversions and heavier traffic around the event, and give any cross-town trip on 13 November extra time.

moved.what: The Hindu reports Deepavali special trains between Bengaluru, Mangaluru and Goa on 7 and 8 November, and a request for extra Bengaluru-Mangaluru services for the festival rush.
moved.so_what: If you are travelling for the festival, book the special on those dates now. A request for extra services is not a confirmed service, so do not plan around it.

moved.what: The Times of India reports a gas cylinder exploding in Bengaluru after leaking gas caught flame from an oil lamp; the delivery worker escaped without serious injuries.
moved.so_what: During Deepavali, keep lit lamps away from the kitchen and the cylinder. If you smell gas, open windows and leave the lamp and switches alone before you call anyone.

moved.what: The Times of India reports that a woman posing as a police officer promised to help a 75-year-old vendor recover his wife's missing gold chain, collected ₹40,000 over three months, then transferred ₹1.6 lakh from his phone and fled.
moved.so_what: Anyone who offers to recover something lost for a fee, or asks to handle your phone, is the signal. Genuine police do not charge for recovery or ask to operate your UPI app.
